lead: A switch moves at t = 0. The inductor current and the capacitor voltage cannot change in zero time, because that would need a jump in the stored energy ½Li² or ½Cv², and so infinite power. So the state just before switching, at t = 0⁻, fixes the state just after, at t = 0⁺, and everything after that is an ordinary resistive circuit problem. This one idea starts every transient problem correctly, from the inductor in a phone charger to the capacitor that holds up a router through a Chennai power cut.
prereq: You need: the V-I relations of R, L and C, and KVL and KCL, from circuit elements and laws.

blocks.text: Three instants matter. At t = 0⁻ the circuit is still in its old state, at t = 0 the switch moves, and at t = 0⁺ the new circuit has just started. The signs are not arithmetic: they mean the left and right limits of time around the switching instant.

An inductor stores energy ½Li<sub>L</sub>², where L is the inductance in henries and i<sub>L</sub> the current through it in amperes. A jump in i<sub>L</sub> would change that energy in zero time, which needs infinite power. No real source supplies that, so the inductor current is continuous. A capacitor stores ½Cv<sub>C</sub>², with C in farads and v<sub>C</sub> in volts, and the same argument makes the capacitor voltage continuous.
Everything else may jump. The inductor voltage can change instantly, so can the capacitor current, and a resistor has no memory at all: it obeys Ohm's law at every instant.
Both are measured with the reference direction and polarity chosen before the switch.

sections.h3: The equivalent circuit at 0⁺ and at ∞

blocks.text: At t = 0⁺ replace the inductor by a current source of value i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻), pointing the way the current flowed, and the capacitor by a voltage source of value v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻), with the same polarity. What is left is a resistive circuit: solve it with KVL and KCL.
At t → ∞ with a DC source the circuit settles. Then v<sub>L</sub> = L di/dt = 0, so the inductor is a short circuit, and i<sub>C</sub> = C dv/dt = 0, so the capacitor is an open circuit.

items: Draw the circuit for t < 0 with the switch in its old position; with DC, L is a short and C is open. Find i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻) and v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻).
Carry them across the switch unchanged.
Draw the t = 0⁺ circuit with L as a current source and C as a voltage source, and find the currents and voltages you need.
Draw the t → ∞ circuit with L short and C open, and find the final values.

blocks.text: If nothing was stored, the two pictures look like opposites: at 0⁺ a 0 A inductor source is an open branch and a 0 V capacitor source is a short, while at ∞ the inductor is a short and the capacitor is open. Keep the two instants apart.

The end values fix where the answer starts and stops; the first slope tells you how it leaves. Read the element laws v<sub>L</sub> = L di<sub>L</sub>/dt and i<sub>C</sub> = C dv<sub>C</sub>/dt at t = 0⁺:

blocks.where: in A/s, with v<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) from KVL on the 0⁺ circuit.
in V/s, with i<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) from KCL on the 0⁺ circuit.

blocks.text: Neither vL nor iC is continuous, so both are found fresh after the switch. In a second-order circuit the initial value and this first slope are the two conditions that fix the two constants of the solution (see second-order circuits). They also let you sketch the answer before any algebra and catch a wrong one.

figure.caption: Top: the worked example before the switch, with the inductor carrying 2 A and the capacitor holding 6 V. Bottom left: just after S closes, the inductor acts as a 2 A source and the capacitor as a 6 V source, so 4 V appears across L. Bottom right: long after, L is a short and C is open.

spec.aria: Three views of one circuit: a 10 volt source, R1 2 ohms with a switch across it, L 1 henry, and C 0.25 farad in parallel with R2 3 ohms. Before the switch i L is 2 amperes and v C is 6 volts; at 0 plus L is a 2 ampere source and C a 6 volt source; at infinity L is a short, C is open, i L is 3.33 amperes and v C is 10 volts.

examples.question: In the circuit of Figure 5.1.1, a 10 V DC source feeds R₁ = 2 Ω and L = 1 H in series to node a. From node a to the return line sit C = 0.25 F and R₂ = 3 Ω in parallel. The circuit has been in this state for a long time. At t = 0 a switch S across R₁ closes and shorts it out. Find i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺), v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺), i<sub>C</sub>(0⁺), v<sub>L</sub>(0⁺), the two first slopes, and the final values i<sub>L</sub>(∞) and v<sub>C</sub>(∞).
steps: Before the switch. DC steady state: L is a short and C is open, so one current flows through R₁, L and R₂: 10/(2 + 3) = 2 A. So iL(0⁻) = 2 A, and C sits across R₂: vC(0⁻) = 2 × 3 = 6 V.
Across the switch. iL(0⁺) = 2 A and vC(0⁺) = 6 V.
The 0⁺ circuit. R₁ is shorted, L is a 2 A current source and C is a 6 V source. R₂ has 6 V across it, so its current is 6/3 = 2 A.
Capacitor current. KCL at node a: iL = iC + iR2, so iC(0⁺) = 2 − 2 = 0 A.
Inductor voltage. KVL round the source, L and C: 10 = vL(0⁺) + 6, so vL(0⁺) = 4 V. It was 0 V before the switch: the inductor voltage jumped, which is allowed.
First slopes. diL/dt = 4/1 = 4 A/s. dvC/dt = 0/0.25 = 0 V/s, so vC leaves 6 V with a flat start.
Final state. L short, C open, R₁ still shorted: iL(∞) = 10/3 = 3.33 A and vC(∞) = 3.33 × 3 = 10 V.
examples.answer: i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = 2 A, v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = 6 V, i<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = 0 A, v<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = 4 V, di<sub>L</sub>/dt = 4 A/s, dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = 0 V/s, i<sub>L</sub>(∞) = 3.33 A, v<sub>C</sub>(∞) = 10 V.
examples.check:
V=10; R1=2; R2=3; L=1; C=0.25
iL0=V/(R1+R2); vC0=iL0*R2
iR2=vC0/R2; iC=iL0-iR2; vL=V-vC0
print(iL0,vC0,iC,vL,vL/L,iC/C,V/R2,V)

traps: Treating L as an open and C as a short at t = 0⁺ in every case. In general they are sources of value i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻) and v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻); they look like an open and a short only when nothing was stored. The unconditional short/open rule belongs to DC steady state.
Believing a big source forces i<sub>L</sub> or v<sub>C</sub> to jump. Only an impulse could; a finite source gives a finite slope, not a jump.
Applying continuity to the wrong variable: inductor voltage, capacitor current and every resistor quantity may jump.
Solving the t < 0 circuit with the switch already in its new position, so the stored values are wrong from the first line.
Unit slips: di/dt = v<sub>L</sub>/L is in A/s only with v<sub>L</sub> in volts and L in henries; forgetting to convert mH gives a factor of 1000.

quiz.q: Which two quantities cannot change instantaneously in a circuit driven by finite sources?
quiz.a: The current through an inductor, i<sub>L</sub>, and the voltage across a capacitor, v<sub>C</sub>.

quiz.q: What does an inductor look like in DC steady state, and what does a capacitor look like?
quiz.a: Inductor: a short circuit, v<sub>L</sub> = 0. Capacitor: an open circuit, i<sub>C</sub> = 0.

quiz.q: Why can the current through an inductor not jump? Answer in terms of energy.
quiz.a: The stored energy is ½Li<sub>L</sub>². A jump in i<sub>L</sub> would change it in zero time, which needs infinite power. No finite source can supply that, so i<sub>L</sub> is continuous.

quiz.q: In the worked example the current in R₁ is 2 A at 0⁻ and 0 A at 0⁺. Is this a mistake?
quiz.a: No. R₁ stores no energy, so its current may jump. The closed switch shorts R₁ and carries the whole 2 A inductor current; only i<sub>L</sub> and v<sub>C</sub> must be continuous.

quiz.q: A 10 V DC source feeds R = 5 Ω and L = 0.5 H in series through a switch that closes at t = 0, with i<sub>L</sub>(0⁻) = 0. Find v<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) and di/dt at 0⁺.
quiz.a: i<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = 0 A, so the drop across R is 0 V. KVL: 10 = 0 + v<sub>L</sub>(0⁺), so v<sub>L</sub>(0⁺) = 10 V and di/dt = 10/0.5 = 20 A/s.

quiz.q: A 20 V DC source feeds R = 4 Ω and C = 0.25 F in series through a switch that closes at t = 0, with v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻) = 0. Find i<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) and dv<sub>C</sub>/dt at 0⁺.
quiz.a: At 0⁺ the capacitor is a 0 V source, so the loop current is 20/4 = 5 A = i<sub>C</sub>(0⁺). Then dv<sub>C</sub>/dt = 5/0.25 = 20 V/s.

quiz.q: A 12 V DC source is switched at t = 0 onto R = 6 Ω, L = 2 H and C = 0.5 F in series, with nothing stored. At 0⁺ the full 12 V appears across L although v<sub>C</sub> = 0 and i = 0. Explain, and find di/dt at 0⁺, i(∞) and v<sub>C</sub>(∞).
quiz.a: Continuity gives v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = 0 V and i(0⁺) = 0 A, so the drops across C and R are zero and KVL puts all 12 V on L. Then di/dt = 12/2 = 6 A/s: the current climbs steeply but continuously. At t → ∞ the capacitor is open, so i(∞) = 0 A and v<sub>C</sub>(∞) = 12 V.

beyond: In real hardware these initial conditions decide whether a device survives being plugged in. A large capacitor in a laptop adapter looks like a short at t = 0⁺, so designers add a precharge resistor or an NTC thermistor to limit the inrush current; electric-vehicle battery packs use a precharge contactor for the same reason. Circuit simulators such as SPICE accept these initial conditions directly. Search next: inrush current, precharge circuit, RC snubber.
